newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin slams tax dodgers as budget faces defeat.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin slams tax dodgers as budget faces defeat.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin condemned tax-dodging big business for Russia's economic crisis on Thursday, a day before parliament, dominated by his Communist opponents, was set to throw out the government's 1997 budget.

Yeltsin, who has stepped up his workload this week, met his chief-of-staff Anatoly Chubais for about an hour at the Barvikha sanatorium outside Moscow, where the 65-year-old Kremlin leader is preparing for a heart bypass operation.
A Kremlin statement released after the meeting said Yeltsin ordered government officials to declare their income for 1996 and called the current wage situation unacceptable.

"Students, teachers, the military and other workers in the state sphere are not receiving wages because a number of big enterprises are literally taking the finances of the country by the throat and refusing to pay taxes," Yeltsin said.

Scientists demonstrated in Moscow on Thursday, saying Russian research was in a state of collapse. Their protest followed similar pleas from the nation's cultural elite, teachers, pensioners and many other groups.
Workers in many sectors have not been paid for months.
Yeltsin's meeting with Chubais was the latest of a number of discussions with officials since he moved from a Moscow hospital last weekend. The operation is due within a couple of months.
The president will address the nation on the radio on Friday morning, his second such broadcast in eight days.

It will coincide with the first reading of the government's 1997 budget in the lower house of parliament, the State Duma, where the opposition Communists and their allies dominate the chamber with more than 200 of the 450 seats.
The budget is virtually certain to be rejected, forcing the government to enter discussions on modifications.

"The budget doesn't correspond to those main messages which were in the (government) statement when (parliament) confirmed its appointment," Communist Party leader Gennady Zyuganov told Russian Television.
Among the campaign promises which helped Yeltsin beat Zyuganov in July's presidential election was a pledge that the government would pay pensioners and state employees in full.
Even the government party set up by Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, Our Home is Russia, wants the budget reviewed.
Itar-Tass news agency quoted a Kremlin source saying the president may speak at length on the radio on wage arrears.
In last Thursday's address, Yeltsin told Russians they still had a working president and not to write him off too soon.
Despite that, financial markets have been buffeted this week by rumours that Yeltsin was seriously ill or even dead.

But television film released by the Kremlin showed him smiling, gesturing and chatting for about a minute with Chubais, the 41-year-old liberal economist who controls the powerful presidential administration during Yeltsin's absence.
Michael DeBakey, the eminent U.S. heart surgeon who is part of the team preparing the operation, told Reuters in Houston, Texas late on Wednesday: "Everything is still fine."
In another side of confidence in Yeltsin's health, his press service said he spoke to Belarus President Alexander Lukashenko spoke by telephone and agreed to meet next Wednesday in Moscow.
